briefing: Brent crude ended October near US$118 after more tanker attacks near Hormuz, while Statistics Canada says the economy stalled in August just as the Bank of Canada raised rates. Ontario's fall update lifted this year's deficit to $16.9 billion and pushed balance to 2029-30, and a revised list of 50% U.S. tariffs took effect Friday. Americans vote Tuesday with Senate control a toss-up; clocks fall back an hour early Sunday. In Toronto, police are still seeking suspects after a violent home invasion in the Bridle Path.
headline: Oil tops US$117 as Ontario's deficit swells to $16.9B

keyDates.why: Control of Congress decides how much room Trump has on tariffs and the Iran war.

stories.backstory: The U.S. and Israel began striking Iran on Feb. 28, and Iran responded by choking traffic through the Strait of Hormuz, the route for about a fifth of the world's oil. A June peace memorandum briefly reopened the strait, but it collapsed in July and the U.S. imposed a blockade on Iranian shipping. Yemen's Houthis have since widened the fight with missile attacks on Saudi Arabia, and Egypt's parliament has authorized sending troops to help the Saudis. Qatar handed Iran a new draft deal on Oct. 25, which Tehran said contained ideas it could not accept.
stories.headline: Brent tops US$117 as two more tankers are hit near Hormuz
stories.impact: Expect GTA gas and diesel prices to stay high, which feeds into grocery, delivery and transit costs. Alberta oil revenues rise, but Ontario households and manufacturers mostly feel the cost side.
stories.now: Brent crude settled about 2.4% higher at US$117.64 a barrel on Friday and U.S. benchmark WTI closed at US$104.12, leaving Brent up roughly 15% for October and at its highest level since April. Iran's Revolutionary Guard said one tanker struck a naval mine while using an unauthorized route, while the U.K. Maritime Trade Operations agency said another was hit by explosives that a small boat attached to its hull. President Trump said he expects the nine-month war to end soon but gave no details, after earlier saying the U.S. would not strike before Tuesday's midterms. Qatari mediators returned to Tehran to keep working on a deal, and U.S. Central Command puts the war's cost at no less than US$47 billion.

stories.summary: Oil posted its fourth straight monthly gain on Friday after two tankers were damaged in the Strait of Hormuz within a day and Washington kept the option of new strikes on Iran open.

stories.why: Oil near US$118 is the main force behind higher inflation in Canada and the U.S., and it pushed the Bank of Canada into a rate hike this week. Any U.S. strike after the midterms could send prices higher still.

stories.backstory: Broad Canada-U.S. trade talks collapsed in August, and Trump then imposed 50% tariffs on about $20 billion of Canadian goods, prompting Canadian counter-tariffs. Since then the White House has repeatedly adjusted which products are covered, easing some farm and forestry goods while adding others. Separate U.S. tariffs on steel, aluminum and autos under a national-security law (Section 232) hit Ontario's factories hardest. Sources said this week a narrower deal on steel and autos was possible before the midterms, but U.S. officials want more concessions.
stories.headline: New U.S. tariff list takes effect as Ottawa reports little progress
stories.impact: Factory jobs in Windsor, Oshawa, Hamilton and the GTA's parts plants remain exposed. Some imported goods such as paint, rugs and air conditioners may cost more if Canada responds or suppliers pass on costs.
stories.now: From Oct. 30, the U.S. dropped plywood, plastic wrap, cardboard boxes and some food machinery from its 50% tariff list on Canadian goods but added items including cocoa powder, paint, fibreboard (MDF), carpets and rugs, air conditioners and canoes. A Canadian official told Reuters on Wednesday that discussions continue but progress has been limited, while Prime Minister Mark Carney said Canada will sign only a deal that works for both countries. Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick and Canada's trade minister Dominic LeBlanc remain in regular contact on steel (taxed at up to 50%) and autos (25%). Trump has said he will raise steel and auto tariffs on Canada to 50% on Jan. 1, and an importer has filed the first court challenge to the August tariffs.

stories.summary: A reshuffled list of Canadian goods facing 50% U.S. tariffs took effect Friday, while a Canadian official said talks on steel and auto duties have made only limited progress.

stories.why: Ontario sells most of its steel and auto output to the U.S., and the province says steel exports there have fallen by more than half since 2024. The midterm result could change how willing Washington is to bargain.

stories.backstory: Ontario's spring budget had already forecast a deficit near $13.8 billion as U.S. tariffs hit steel and auto exports. The province's steel exports to the U.S. fell to $4.1 billion in the first eight months of 2026 from $8.4 billion in the same period of 2024. Ottawa and Ontario announced an $8.7-billion action plan for steel, autos and critical minerals in October. The legislature returned on Oct. 27 after a 21-week break.
stories.headline: Ontario deficit grows to $16.9 billion; balance pushed to 2029-30
stories.impact: Most homes use about 700 kWh a month, so the rebate cap mainly affects heavy electricity users from May 2027. Businesses investing in equipment get faster write-offs, and buyers of newly built homes keep the HST break.
stories.now: Thursday's fall economic statement projects a $16.9-billion deficit for 2026-27, up from $13.8 billion in the spring budget, followed by shortfalls of $12.7 billion and $6.7 billion before a $200-million surplus in 2029-30. The province now expects growth of just 0.5% this year and 1.5% in 2027, with unemployment at 7.2% this year. New and confirmed measures include an $8-billion business write-off matching Ottawa's, about $8 billion more for health care by decade's end, and a nearly $4-billion top-up to the contingency fund for more tariffs. The Ontario Electricity Rebate will be capped at 1,200 kWh a month for homes starting May 2027, and the $4-billion Protect Ontario Investment Fund is paused. Opposition parties called the update weak on affordability.

sources.title: CP24: Ontario deficit grows to $16.9 billion
Global News: $36B in deficits over 3 years

stories.summary: Finance Minister Peter Bethlenfalvy's fall update raised this year's deficit by more than $3 billion and delayed a balanced budget by a year as the trade war slows growth.
stories.why: A bigger deficit and slower growth limit room for new programs and tax relief, and confirm the trade war is hurting Ontario more than other provinces.

stories.backstory: The Bank of Canada cut to 2.25% in October 2025 and then held for seven meetings. Oil prices driven up by the Iran war lifted September inflation to 3.1%, even as Canada lost 68,000 jobs that month. The bank's new forecast puts 2027 inflation at 3.1%, well above its 2% target. Flat growth and rising rates together raise the risk of stagflation, meaning weak growth with high inflation.
stories.headline: Economy stalls in August, two days after Bank of Canada's hike
stories.impact: Variable-rate mortgages and lines of credit already cost more after the hike. A weak economy could slow hiring in the GTA, so it is a good moment to review budgets and renewal plans.
stories.now: Real gross domestic product (GDP) was unchanged in August, missing the 0.2% gain economists expected, with retail up 1.2% but wholesale trade and car-and-parts manufacturing down. StatCan's early estimate shows a 0.1% drop in September as manufacturing and oil and gas output fell, leaving third-quarter growth at about 0.3%. That follows Wednesday's quarter-point hike to 2.50%, which the Bank of Canada made to keep high oil prices from spreading through the economy, while signalling more could be needed. Premier Doug Ford called the hike a massive mistake, and Ontario's fall update now sees provincial growth of only 0.5% this year.

stories.summary: Statistics Canada says the economy was flat in August and probably shrank 0.1% in September, a weak backdrop for the Bank of Canada's first rate increase since 2023.

timeline.event: Rate cut to 2.25%; seven holds follow
August GDP flat; September seen down 0.1%

stories.why: The data shows the bank raising rates into a stalling economy, a tough trade-off that makes its next moves less predictable.

stories.headline: Police seek suspects after violent Bridle Path home invasion; family asks for privacy
stories.summary: A Toronto real estate company CEO and his two adult daughters were shot, and the family was beaten, in a home invasion early Thursday. Police are still looking for suspects.
stories.now: Early Thursday morning, intruders attacked a family inside their home in the Bridle Path neighbourhood of North York. Outlets including CityNews and the Canadian Press report that the CEO of a Toronto real estate company and his two adult daughters were shot and that hammers were used in the assault; the injured father has since described the family as traumatized and asked for privacy. Toronto police have released suspect descriptions and say the investigation is continuing. No arrests had been reported in the coverage reviewed for this edition.
stories.backstory: The attack was first reported on Thursday as a home invasion and shooting at a Bridle Path residence that sent four people to hospital. Later reports named the family's roles and described the injuries, and police appealed publicly for tips. The Bridle Path is one of Toronto's wealthiest residential areas, which is why the case drew national and international attention.

timeline.event: Home invasion and shooting reported at a Bridle Path home; four taken to hospital
Injured father speaks out and asks for privacy

stories.why: Violent home invasions are rare in the area and this one has drawn national attention. It raises questions about residential security and policing in wealthier neighbourhoods.
stories.impact: Police say the investigation is active, so residents of North York and nearby areas may see a stronger police presence. Anyone with information or doorbell or security video from the area is likely to be asked to contact Toronto Police.

stories.backstory: Republicans have held both chambers of Congress since January 2025. All 435 House seats and about a third of the Senate are on the ballot on Nov. 3. Tariffs and high gas prices tied to the Iran war have hurt Trump's approval, which Reuters recently put at 32%. Recent national polls have given Democrats a lead on the generic ballot.
stories.headline: Senate control a toss-up as midterms enter final weekend
stories.impact: The outcome will shape U.S. tariff policy on Canadian steel and autos and the timing of any strikes on Iran, both of which affect Ontario jobs and fuel prices.
stories.now: Fox News' power rankings now call the Senate a toss-up, moving Ohio to lean Democrat and South Carolina to toss-up. In Michigan, Democrat Abdul El-Sayed faces Republican Mike Rogers, and in Texas Republican Ken Paxton faces Democrat James Talarico. Michael Bloomberg added about US$36 million for Democrats, bringing his late spending to roughly US$116 million. Trump rallied in Florida on Friday and plans rallies in Iowa and Kansas on Sunday, while in Alaska the Justice Department asked for some ballots to be set aside amid probes involving a similarly named candidate.

stories.summary: With Election Day on Tuesday, forecasters see control of the U.S. Senate hinging on about six states, and both parties are pouring in late money.

stories.why: A Democratic Congress could check Trump's tariffs and war powers, while Republican control would give him a freer hand for the next two years.

stories.backstory: The Justice Department sued California on Oct. 15, alleging that more than 20,000 registered voters are likely noncitizens. U.S. elections are run by states, and the Constitution gives them primary control over how they are held. The administration has pressed several states over voter rolls ahead of the midterms.
stories.headline: Appeals court again blocks Trump bid to set aside 20,000 California ballots
stories.impact: Little direct effect in Ontario, but disputes over vote counting could delay results in close races that decide control of Congress.
stories.now: A three-judge panel of the 9th Circuit ruled 2-1 that setting the ballots aside would violate the Constitution's Elections Clause and risk disenfranchising eligible voters. Judges Mark Bennett and Gabriel Sanchez formed the majority, while Judge Patrick Bumatay dissented, calling the request reasonable. It was the second appellate rejection in less than a week, after a district judge also ruled against the administration on Wednesday.

sources.title: Al Jazeera: Appeals court rejects bid on California ballots

stories.summary: A federal appeals panel on Friday refused the Justice Department's request to stop California from counting about 20,000 mail ballots it says may come from noncitizens.

timeline.event: First appeal rejected on procedural grounds
District court rules against the administration

stories.why: The ruling sets limits on how far federal officials can intervene in state-run elections days before a national vote.

stories.backstory: The Fed raised rates in September for the first time in three years as the Iran war pushed oil above US$100 a barrel. Tech giants have spent heavily on artificial intelligence (AI), and those stocks have driven much of the market's swings this month. Strong U.S. growth paired with high energy prices keeps pressure on the Fed not to cut.
stories.headline: U.S. economy grows 3.4% in third quarter as inflation cools
stories.impact: Canadian fixed mortgage rates follow bond yields, so they are unlikely to fall soon. Strong U.S. demand helps Ontario exporters that are not hit by tariffs.
stories.now: The Bureau of Economic Analysis said real GDP grew at a 3.4% annual rate in the third quarter, up from 2.2% in the second, driven by business investment in equipment and computers, inventory building and consumer spending. The personal consumption expenditures (PCE) price index rose at a 2.1% rate, down from 5.0%, and core PCE, which excludes food and energy, eased to 2.5%. The data came a day after the Federal Reserve held its key rate at 3.75% to 4% in a 10-2 vote, with Lisa Cook and Beth Hammack favouring a hike. Gold fell to a one-year low on Friday as investors bet rates will stay high.

Bloomberg: Fed holds rates
The National: Gold falls to one-year low

stories.summary: The U.S. economy expanded at a 3.4% annual rate from July to September, faster than the spring, while a key inflation gauge eased.

timeline.event: Fed raises rates for first time in three years
Fed holds 10-2; two votes for a hike

stories.why: A strong U.S. economy and a hawkish Fed tend to keep bond yields up on both sides of the border.

stories.backstory: Canada joined the EU's SAFE defence procurement program in February as Ottawa looked to diversify away from the U.S. A Canada-EU trade deal (CETA) has been in force provisionally since 2017. The term 'associate member' was dropped from a draft statement days before the summit. Carney also visited the United Arab Emirates this month to expand trade ties.
stories.headline: Canada and EU launch 'Alliance for the Future' and aim for associate ties
stories.impact: Nothing changes right away, but over time it could open more European markets to Ontario firms and widen work and study options for young people.
stories.now: Carney and European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen launched an 'Alliance for the Future' focused on AI, energy, critical minerals and quantum technology. Both backed the idea of Canada as the EU's first 'associate' member, though the final joint statement used the phrase 'ever-closer association' after some member states asked for more time. Carney said the substance will be worked out in coming months, plans to attend a June meeting of European leaders, and the sides aim to define the concept by the 2027 summit. He said it could make it easier for young Canadians to live, study and travel in Europe.

sources.title: TIME: Carney sets target for EU 'associate' status
National Observer: Carney, von der Leyen both want associate membership
Council of the EU: EU-Canada summit, 29-30 October 2026

stories.summary: Carney and EU leaders wrapped a two-day summit in Montreal by starting work on a closer partnership short of full membership, with a goal of defining it by next year.

timeline.event: Canada-EU trade deal provisionally in force
Canada joins EU's SAFE defence program

stories.why: It is Canada's biggest step yet to tie its economy and security more closely to Europe amid the U.S. trade war.

stories.backstory: Israelis voted on Oct. 27 amid an eight-month war with Iran that has reshaped regional politics. Netanyahu's outgoing coalition held 60 seats when the last Knesset dissolved in July. Arab parties won more seats than in any previous election, making them potential kingmakers.
stories.headline: Final count leaves Netanyahu's bloc at 53 seats, short of a majority
stories.impact: Indirect for Ontario, mainly through oil prices and the wider conflict's effect on inflation.
stories.now: Final results give Benjamin Netanyahu's right-wing and religious bloc 53 of 120 seats and the opposition bloc led by Gadi Eisenkot 48, with Arab-led parties holding the balance. Likud figures alleged fraud, but the Central Elections Committee said the vote was lawful and there was no basis for claims of election theft. The Joint List said it is ready to help form an alternative government, and Ra'am leader Mansour Abbas said he has talked with both sides. Results are due to be certified on Nov. 4, after which President Isaac Herzog consults parties.

stories.summary: Israel faces weeks of coalition talks after final results gave neither Netanyahu's bloc nor Gadi Eisenkot's a 61-seat majority, and Likud claimed the vote was stolen.

timeline.event: Israel votes; exit polls show no majority
Final results: 53 vs 48; Likud alleges fraud

stories.why: Who governs Israel will shape whether the war with Iran escalates or winds down.

stories.backstory: Russia's full-scale invasion began in February 2022, and both sides now regularly strike each other's energy sites. A local humanitarian ceasefire began in occupied Oleshky in Kherson region on Oct. 27, and a Ukrainian delegation arrived there on Oct. 30. U.S. envoy Steve Witkoff met Putin on Oct. 21 as Washington pushes for new talks.
stories.headline: U.S. approves 500 Patriot missiles for Ukraine as Russia keeps up strikes
stories.impact: Canada is a major donor to Ukraine; the war also keeps European energy markets tight, adding to global fuel prices.
stories.now: Russia launched ballistic missiles, four cruise missiles and 113 drones overnight into Oct. 30, according to the Institute for the Study of War, and Ukraine asked for an emergency UN Security Council meeting. The U.S. State Department approved the sale of 500 Patriot PAC-3 missiles, though President Zelensky warned deliveries may take years. At a G20 foreign ministers' meeting in Atlanta on Friday, Russian Foreign Minister Sergei Lavrov said Moscow's position is unchanged. Zelensky hopes for three-way talks with the U.S. in Abu Dhabi between Nov. 6 and 10.

stories.summary: Washington cleared the sale of 500 Patriot air-defence missiles to Kyiv as Russia fired more than 100 drones and several missiles overnight, while Moscow signalled no change in its war aims.

timeline.event: Lavrov at G20 meeting: position unchanged

stories.why: Talks in early November could be the first real test of a ceasefire path since early this year.

stories.backstory: Ohio-based Cleveland-Cliffs bought Stelco in 2024 and made binding job commitments under the Investment Canada Act. U.S. 50% tariffs on Canadian steel took effect in August, idling some Hamilton lines. Ottawa has threatened legal action and even a forced sale if the company breaks its promises, and set a 15-day deadline on Oct. 22.
stories.headline: Stelco owner hopes to recall 175 Hamilton workers before Christmas
stories.impact: Hamilton steel families and suppliers face uncertainty into the holidays. The 15-day deadline runs out around Nov. 6.
stories.now: Goncalves said 175 workers have been laid off, all at the Hamilton plant, fewer than the up to 500 Stelco warned of in September, and none yet at Lake Erie Works. He said he hopes to recall all of them before Christmas if a plan to sell more Canadian-made steel works, and that he will not sell Stelco for at least a year. Industry Minister Mélanie Joly says she won't meet him without a concrete rehiring plan and timeline, and Ottawa is consulting lawyers about his comment that he bought Stelco to protect U.S. operations. The Steelworkers union accuses the company of using workers as leverage.

stories.summary: Cleveland-Cliffs CEO Lourenco Goncalves says he wants to bring back the laid-off Stelco workers by Christmas if Canadian steel sales pick up, while Ottawa keeps up its legal threats.

timeline.event: U.S. 50% tariffs on Canadian steel take effect

stories.why: It tests whether Ottawa can enforce foreign-takeover promises when tariffs squeeze an industry.

stories.backstory: Toronto uses traffic agents to direct vehicles at busy intersections near construction zones and during rush hour. The Thorncliffe Park area around Millwood and Overlea sees heavy truck traffic. Careless driving causing death is a provincial offence, not a Criminal Code charge.
stories.headline: Dump truck driver charged after Toronto traffic agent killed
stories.impact: Drivers in construction zones should watch for traffic agents and follow their directions; expect continued scrutiny of turning trucks in dense neighbourhoods.
stories.now: Police say a southbound dump truck turning left from Millwood Road onto Overlea Boulevard hit the 42-year-old agent around 9 a.m. Thursday, and he died at the scene. The 33-year-old driver stayed and co-operated, and was charged with careless driving causing death under the Highway Traffic Act. He is due in court on Jan. 28, and police are asking for dashcam or security video. Mayor Olivia Chow identified the victim later Thursday.

stories.summary: A Brampton man faces a careless driving charge after a City of Toronto traffic agent was struck and killed while directing traffic in the east end.

timeline.event: Agent struck and killed at Millwood and Overlea
Driver charged with careless driving causing death

stories.why: It is a rare death of a city worker on traffic duty and adds to pressure for stricter truck safety rules.

stories.backstory: Chow first won a 2023 by-election with 37% after John Tory resigned, and this was her first run as an incumbent. Bradford, a Beaches-East York councillor, ran on a first-year property-tax freeze and scrapping Toronto's land transfer tax on homes under $1.1 million, while Chow promised cheaper groceries, school lunches and more affordable housing. Mississauga's race pitted Parrish, elected in a 2024 by-election, against Crombie, who returned after leading the Ontario Liberals. All Ontario municipalities voted on the same day for four-year terms.
stories.headline: Chow re-elected; GTA voters oust mayors in Mississauga, Hamilton, Oakville and Milton
stories.impact: Toronto homeowners should expect Chow's budget approach to continue rather than Bradford's proposed tax freeze, and Mississauga residents can watch for Tedjo's promised two-year freeze on the residential tax levy. Ward councillor and school trustee results are posted on each city's website.
stories.now: Chow finished with about 54% to Brad Bradford's 41%, a margin of more than 127,000 votes, and carried 19 of Toronto's 25 wards after polls had suggested a close race; ballots counted by 10 p.m. were roughly double the 563,124 cast in 2022. Alvin Tedjo unseated Carolyn Parrish in Mississauga, and in Hamilton Keanin Loomis won with about 41% while Andrea Horwath fell to third at 14%. In Halton, Jeff Knoll took Oakville with 36% over incumbent Rob Burton, and George Minakakis beat Milton's long-time mayor Gord Krantz 45% to about 25%; Christina Early won Caledon with 59%. Patrick Brown (Brampton), Steven Del Duca (Vaughan), Frank Scarpitti (Markham) and David West (Richmond Hill) were re-elected, while Oshawa, Clarington and Ajax chose new mayors.
